answer:
Using the effective annual discount rate \(d\), the present value of the instalment plan is

\[
120+120(1-d)+120(1-d)^2.
\]

Set this equal to the immediate payment \(327\):

\[
120\bigl[1+(1-d)+(1-d)^2\bigr]=327.
\]

Let \(x=1-d\). Then

\[
120(1+x+x^2)=327
\]
\[
x^2+x-\frac{69}{40}=0.
\]

The positive solution is

\[
x=\frac{\sqrt{79/10}-1}{2}\approx 0.90534693.
\]

Thus

\[
d=1-x\approx 0.0946531,
\]

so the break-even annual discount rate is

\[
d^*\approx 9.4653\%.
\]

At \(d=0\), the instalment PV is

\[
120+120+120=360>327,
\]

so below the break-even rate the lump sum is cheaper. Since increasing the discount rate lowers the PV of future payments, for

\[
d>9.4653\%
\]

the instalment plan has present value less than \(327\), so it is cheaper. For example, at \(d=15\%\),

\[
PV=120[1+0.85+0.85^2]=308.70<327.
\]

So the instalment plan is cheaper for \(d>9.4653\%\) approximately.

If instead “discount rate” means the annual interest rate \(r\) used as \(1/(1+r)^t\), then the break-even rate is

\[
r^*\approx 10.4549\%,
\]

and the instalment plan is cheaper for \(r>10.4549\%\).
